'''Muthu Alagappan''' (born {{Circa|1990}}<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/><ref name="Forbes 2012 30 Under 30: Sports"/>) is a former medical resident known for his [[National Basketball Association|professional basketball]] analytics. He was born in England and raised in Texas. During college at [[Stanford University]], he began an internship at [[big data]] [[startup company]] Ayasdi, where he used their software on [[basketball]] statistics to determine 13 distinct [[basketball positions|positions of play]]. After he spoke at the 2012 [[MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference]], several professional teams began to use the company's software. He was given the top prize at the conference, and ''[[GQ]]'' called his work both "a new frontier for the NBA" and "Muthuball"—an allusion to [[Sabermetrics|Moneyball]] [[baseball]] [[statistical analysis]] known for revolutionizing the sport.<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/> ''[[Forbes]]'' included him in their 2012 and 2013  "[[Forbes 30 Under 30|30 Under 30]]" list of influential people in the sports industry. His work has received mention in ''[[The New York Times]]'', [[ESPN]], ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'', ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'', and ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]''.

== Early life ==

Alagappan was born in [[Crewe, England]], and raised in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]], US.<ref name="Forbes 2012 30 Under 30: Sports" /><ref name="Tamil Culture interview"/> He is of [[Tamils|Tamil]] heritage.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> He graduated from [[Stanford University]] in 2012 with a degree in biomechanical engineering<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/><ref name="TEDx Spokane"/> and the [[Stanford Medical School]] in 2016.<ref>[https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2016/06/dont-despair-in-the-face-of-failure-biochemist-tells-grads.html Don’t despair in the face of failure, biochemist tells grads]</ref>  {{as of|2017}}, he was an internal medicine resident at [[Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Profile|url=https://resident360.nejm.org/profiles/muthu-alagappan|website=NEJM Resident 360|access-date=19 January 2018}}</ref> Alagappan is a longtime [[Houston Rockets]] fan.<ref name="Forbes 2012 30 Under 30: Sports"/>

== Basketball analytics ==

Alagappan was hired as an [[intern]] with Ayasdi, a [[big data]] [[startup company|startup]] in [[Palo Alto, California]], through Stanford's Mayfield Fellows Program, where he was hired to do sales.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> He tested the company's software on basketball stats and called the output "the true positions of the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]]".<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/> The [[topological data analysis]] mapped similarities between NBA players and identified 13 distinct [[Basketball positions|positions of play]], as opposed to the traditional five.<ref name="NYT: Trading Small Forward"/> Those traditional positions, such as [[Power forward (basketball)|power forward]] and [[shooting guard]], have become ambiguous and outmoded as a result of the increased variety of player styles categorized by them.<ref name="NYT: Trading Small Forward"/> Alagappan's method groups professional basketball players by statistical strengths and places them into the new positional model.<ref name="Forbes 2012 30 Under 30: Sports"/>

He started with a collection of seven basic statistics ([[Assist (basketball)|assists]], [[Block (basketball)|blocks]], [[Assist (basketball)|fouls]], [[Point (basketball)|points]], [[Rebound (basketball)|rebounds]], [[Steal (basketball)|steals]], and [[Turnover (basketball)|turnovers]]) from [[Yahoo! Sports]] on every NBA player from the previous season and adjusted the stats for time in play.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> The software grouped the players into color-coded nodes and connected them with lines that represented statistical similarities.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> Alagappan had expected the software to create five groups of nodes by statistical advantages, which would each represent a position of play, but the software instead returned 13 node groups representing 13 mathematically described positions.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> The assignments compare player statistics and not individual style.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> Originally unconfident in his results, he explored the data on his own for a week before sharing his findings with his bosses and basketball statisticians including [[Ken Pomeroy]], who replied in encouragement.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> He then applied and was accepted to speak at the 2012 [[MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference]].<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> By May 2012, at least four NBA teams and one [[Major League Baseball|MLB]] team had contacted Ayasdi about using their technology.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/>

The method is intended to change existing basketball team composition paradigms to help NBA teams win championships.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> Alagappan used [[Devin Ebanks]] of the [[Los Angeles Lakers]] as an example, whom Alagappan considered promising for his classification as a "scoring rebounder" alongside [[Carmelo Anthony]] and [[Dirk Nowitzki]] despite a subpar season record.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> ''[[GQ]]'' reported that Ebanks would come to fulfill the model's forecast in following games for six weeks when two other players sat out and Ebanks [[Starting lineup#Basketball|started]] games.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> While the model couldn't have predicted [[Linsanity]], when given college basketball stats, it was able to determine three players most similar to Lin in college, of which two were already drafted in the NBA.<ref name="Wired: Analytics Reveal 13"/> The forecasting is expected to improve with the growth of the data set.<ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/>

His data-driven analysis has been well received. He won the top prize in the "Evolution of Sports" category at the 2012 [[MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference]].<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/><ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/> ''GQ'' called his work "a new frontier for the NBA" and "Muthuball", an allusion to [[Billy Beane]]'s "[[Moneyball: The Art of Winning an Unfair Game|Moneyball]]" [[sabermetrics]] ([[baseball]] [[statistical analysis]] known for revolutionizing the sport).<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/> ''[[Forbes]]'' included him in their 2012 and 2013 "30 Under 30" lists of influential people in the sports industry.<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/><ref name="Forbes 2012 30 Under 30: Sports"/><ref name="Forbes 2013"/> His work has received mention in ''[[The New York Times]]'', [[ESPN]], ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'', ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'', and ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]''.<ref name="Mercury News: cult status"/><ref name="GQ: Muthuball"/>

Rob Mahoney of ''The New York Times'' called the model "a novel execution of a productive thought", but cited the "one-of-a-kind" catch-all position and the substantial number of players categorized within it as weak points.<ref name="NYT: Trading Small Forward"/> ESPN [[TrueHoop]]'s Jim Calvan criticized Alagappan's Sloan conference presentation for its lack of data showing how team reconfiguration to cover the 13 positions results in more wins.<ref name="ESPN TrueHoop: Solving"/>
